objective.statement: Work out the length of double-dotted notes and rests, and complete bars that hold them.
successCriteria: I know the second dot adds half of what the first dot added.
I can add up a double-dotted note from its parts.
I can use a double-dotted note to complete a bar.

explanation.text: A single dot makes a note half as long again: a dotted minim is a minim plus a crotchet. A second dot adds half of what the first dot added, which is a quarter of the note. So a double-dotted minim is a minim, plus a crotchet, plus a quaver.

music.textAlternative: A double-dotted minim followed by a quaver, in 4/4.

explanation.caption: A double-dotted minim lasts 3½ beats; the quaver completes the bar.

explanation.text: Work in steps. A double-dotted crotchet is a crotchet (1 beat), plus half of it (a quaver, ½ beat), plus a quarter of it (a semiquaver, ¼ beat): 1¾ beats. Its short companion is usually a note that rounds the total up to a whole number of beats, here a semiquaver.

music.textAlternative: A double-dotted crotchet, a semiquaver and a crotchet, in 3/4.
music.questionAlternative: Bar 1: dotted dotted crotchet, semiquaver, crotchet.

explanation.text: Rests can be double-dotted too, with exactly the same length as the note of that name. The reference book points out that a second dot sits awkwardly with the usual rule that each beat should start with a new note or rest, so composers often write such rests another way. In this course you work out the length of a double-dotted rest; you are not asked to decide when to write one.
Each dot adds half of the value before it: note, + ½ note, + ¼ note.

music.textAlternative: A double-dotted crotchet and a semiquaver.

steps: The first dot adds half: a quaver, ½ beat.
The second dot adds half of that: a semiquaver, ¼ beat. The total is 1¾; add the semiquaver and the bar is full.
demonstration.textAlternative: A double-dotted crotchet and a semiquaver fill two beats.

guided.prompt: Which notes added together last as long as a double-dotted quaver?

options.label: a quaver + a semiquaver + a demisemiquaver
a quaver + a semiquaver + a semiquaver

quaver+semiquaver+semiquaver.reason: The second dot adds half of what the first dot added (a demisemiquaver), not another semiquaver.

quaver+semiquaver.reason: That is the value with only one dot. The second dot adds a little more.

quaver+quaver.reason: That is twice the note, far more than two dots add.

hints: Each dot adds half of the value before it.
The first dot adds half the note; the second dot adds half of that.

feedback.correct: Yes: the second dot adds half as much as the first.

mistakes.halved-or-doubled: Each step down the note values halves the length; each step up doubles it.
mistakes.dot-misread: Each dot adds half of the value before it.
mistakes.note-rest-confusion: Check the shape carefully. A rest that hangs below its line lasts longer than one that sits on top of it.
mistakes.tie-dot-confusion: A tie adds separate notes together; a dot adds half the note's own value.
mistakes.tuplet-ignored: Those notes are a tuplet, so they share a different amount of time. Look at the number written over them.

feedback.fallback: Not quite. Try counting each value in crotchet beats.

mastery.completion: The lesson is complete when every step has been answered correctly (retries allowed). Only first-attempt, hint-free independent answers count as mastery evidence; guided steps never do.

provenance.authoredBy: Music Theory Path curriculum team (Brief 05, drafted with AI assistance; pending qualified teacher review)
provenance.notes: Original wording. Follows Grade 4 outcome 3 and First Steps Grade 4 section 2 (pp. 79-80). OPEN QUESTION for the teacher (recorded in the teacher pack): the book says double-dotted rests may be seen where clear but that standard practice avoids them across beats. The course therefore asks only the LENGTH of a double-dotted rest, never writes one into a bar, and never asks whether one is acceptable. Bar questions use double-dotted notes only and have one answer.
